title: The verb stands at the end
goal: Mastering the first verb form — *-на / -нэ / -но / -нө* — and training your ear to a word order that is the reverse of English.
bekal: build full sentences with the verb at the end
use the *-на* form for habits, present situations, and plans
tell *-на* apart from *-ж байна*, which means "right now, at this moment"

dialogs.title: Яриа — Өдөр бүр юу хийдэг вэ?
dialogs.intro: Sarnai and Budi chat in the campus cafeteria about how their days go.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Budi, what time do you get up in the morning?
lines.literal: Budi, you morning how-many hour-at get-up-usually Q?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: At seven. Then I drink tea.
lines.literal: seven hour-at get-up-usually. after -the tea drink-usually.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Sometimes. Usually I just drink tea and go.
lines.literal: sometimes. usually tea only drink-after go.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: How do you get to campus?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: By bus. It takes twenty minutes.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: What do you usually do in the evening?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: I read books at home. Sometimes I watch a movie.
lines.literal: home-at-own book read. sometimes movie watch.

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: What are you doing right now?

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Right now I'm drinking tea. And talking with you.
lines.literal: now I tea drink-ing is. also you-with talk-ing is.

lines.speaker: Буди:
lines.id: Tomorrow I'm going to the museum. Will you come?
lines.literal: tomorrow museum to go. you come Q?

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: Tomorrow I work. Is Saturday OK?
lines.literal: tomorrow I work. Saturday-on may Q?

lines.speaker: Сарнай:
lines.id: OK, that's settled. I'm going to class now.
lines.literal: OK, let's-so. I now lesson-to enter.

notes: ⚠️ **The Mongolian verb always comes last.** Notice that in the fourteen lines of this dialogue, not a single sentence ends with a noun. English says "I drink tea"; Mongolian says "I tea drink". The sentence can't be understood until you reach the end — and that is the listening habit that takes longest to build.

**The -на / -нэ / -но / -нө form covers three things at once: habits, present situations, and plans.** *Би автобусаар явна* can mean "I usually take the bus", "I take the bus", or "I will take the bus". English does something similar — "I'm taking the bus" can be now or tomorrow. **Mongolian has no separate future tense**; context does the work.

**The -даг / -дэг / -дог / -дөг form stresses habit.** *Уншдаг* = "usually reads", *явдаг* = "usually goes". The difference from *-на* is slight: *-даг* stresses routine, *-на* is neutral. When in doubt, use *-на*.

**The -ж / -ч байна form means "right now, at this moment".** *Ууж байна* = is drinking. ⚠️ This is the one place Mongolian really separates "right now" from "usually", and the line is sharp — don't use it for habits.

**Гэртээ and оройдоо use the suffix -даа / -дээ / -доо / -дөө**, meaning "one's own …": *гэртээ* = at one's own home, *оройдоо* = in the evening (of one's day). This suffix is covered in unit 17. For now, accept it as one chunk.

grammars.title: Word order: SOV, and why it makes sense
body: English orders **Subject – Verb – Object**. Mongolian orders **Subject – Object – Verb**. All the extra information — time, place, manner — stands before the verb, and its order among itself is fairly free.

head: English
Монгол
Literally
rows: Tomorrow I'm going to the museum.
I take the bus to school.

after: **The way to practice is not memorizing rules but flipping English sentences out loud.** Take your own sentence, move the verb to the end, and say it. "I eat rice at home" → "I at home rice eat". Do it ten times a day for a week and the habit is set.

⚠️ One consequence that often surprises people: **the question word doesn't move to the front.** *Чи юу хийж байна?* — literally "you what do-ing?", not "what are you doing". The question word stands exactly where its answer will stand. English does this in echo questions ("You're doing what?"), so the pattern isn't entirely foreign.

grammars.title: Forming -на and its relatives
body: From the dictionary form ending in **-х**, drop the *-х*, then add **-на / -нэ / -но / -нө** following vowel harmony. That's all — nothing changes for the person.
after: Look at the second column: the suffix vowel **always** follows the last vowel of the base. *Явах* is back-group → *явна*; *ирэх* is front-group → *ирнэ*; *орох* has *о* → *орно*; *өгөх* has *ө* → *өгнө*. There are no exceptions you need to learn at A1.

⚠️ For the *-ж байна* form, some verbs take **-ч** instead of *-ж*: after *в, г, р, с* and after long vowels. *Өгөх* → *өгч байна*, not *өгж байна*. Say it aloud and you'll choose correctly — *өгж* really is hard to pronounce.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice that **every dictionary form ends in -х**. That's a very handy marker: whenever you see a word ending in *-х* in the dictionary, you know it's a verb. This form also works as a verbal noun — *унших* means both "to read" and "reading", just like English "reading".

Time words almost always stand **at the start of the sentence**, before the subject: *Маргааш би музей рүү явна.* Putting them elsewhere isn't wrong, but the start is the most natural spot — just as in English "Tomorrow I'm going to the museum".

blocks.title: ⚠️ Долоо хоног = week, literally "seven nights"
items: *хоног* means "one full day-and-night cycle", twenty-four whole hours. English has no everyday word for this — the old word "nychthemeron" is all we have.
*Долоо хоног* (seven khonog) = one week. *Хоёр долоо хоног* = two weeks.
*Гурван хоног болно* = "it takes three days" — used for duration, not for dates.

blocks.text: This isn't a table to glance at but one to read aloud from top to bottom, twice. Read the English column, cover the other two, then say the Mongolian before you look. Ten minutes a day for a week is enough.

head: English
Монгол
rows: In the evening I eat meat at home.
She reads a book every day.
Tomorrow we're taking the bus to the market.

blocks.text: Watch how the sentence grows: the verb never leaves the end, and every addition slips in **in front of it**. This is the most useful mental picture for Mongolian — **the verb is the wall at the end of the room, and everything else lines up facing it.**

items: She reads a book at home.
Tomorrow I'm going to the market.
I take the bus every day.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with -на, -нэ, -но, or -нө.
Change into the "right now" form with -ж байна or -ч байна.
Put the words in the right order.
